topics.title: Long ago and now
topics.intro: History is the story of what happened before we were born. Things were very different long ago: no electricity, no cars, no phones!
topics.teach: Explain three ways life was different 100 years ago.
topics.talk: Ask a grandparent what toys they played with, and tell {him} about yours.

topics.title: Roman soldiers in Britain
topics.intro: About 2,000 years ago, the Roman army marched into Britain. Roman soldiers had shields, helmets and clever battle tricks. They built roads, towns and a giant wall.
topics.teach: Explain how the Roman “tortoise” formation worked.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why Roman roads are so straight.

topics.title: Viking raiders
topics.intro: Vikings sailed from Norway, Denmark and Sweden in fast longships. They raided, then many settled down as farmers and traders.
topics.teach: Explain what a longship was like.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which king fought the Vikings (Alfred the Great).

topics.title: 1066: the Battle of Hastings
topics.intro: In 1066 three men wanted to be King of England. It ended with a famous battle near Hastings, and a new king: William the Conqueror.
topics.teach: Explain who won the Battle of Hastings.
topics.talk: Look at pictures of the Bayeux Tapestry together. What can {she} spot?

topics.title: Castles and knights
topics.intro: After 1066, castles were built all over England. Knights in armour protected them. A castle had clever ways to keep enemies out.
topics.teach: Explain three ways a castle kept enemies out.
topics.talk: Visit a castle, or design one together on paper with a moat and drawbridge.

topics.title: The Great Fire of London
topics.intro: In 1666 a fire started in a bakery in London. It spread for four days because the houses were made of wood and built close together.
topics.teach: Explain why the fire spread so quickly.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what Samuel Pepys buried in his garden.

topics.title: Queen Elizabeth I and the Armada
topics.intro: In 1588 a huge Spanish fleet called the Armada sailed to attack England. Queen Elizabeth I’s ships, a clever trick with fire, and stormy weather saved England.
topics.teach: Explain how fireships helped beat the Armada.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how beacons sent a warning across England.

topics.title: Brave nurses: Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole
topics.intro: About 170 years ago, two brave women cared for soldiers in the Crimean War. They changed nursing for ever.
topics.teach: Explain why Florence Nightingale was called “The Lady with the Lamp”.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why keeping hospitals clean saves lives.

topics.title: The First World War and Remembrance
topics.intro: From 1914 to 1918, many countries fought the First World War. Every year on 11 November we wear poppies and stay silent for two minutes to remember the soldiers.
topics.talk: On Remembrance Sunday, talk with {him} about why people are quiet for two minutes.

topics.title: The Second World War at home
topics.intro: From 1939 to 1945, Britain fought in the Second World War. Children were evacuated to the countryside, families had ration books, and Spitfires flew to protect the skies.
topics.talk: Ask an older relative whether their family remembered rationing.

topics.title: Great firsts: flight and the Moon
topics.intro: People have always dreamed of flying. In just 66 years we went from the first aeroplane to walking on the Moon!
topics.teach: Explain what the Wright brothers did.
topics.talk: Ask {him} who was first to walk on the Moon.

topics.title: Wartime heroes: codebreakers, D-Day and brave animals
topics.intro: Some Second World War heroes used their brains, some their boats, and some were even animals! Here are their amazing stories.
topics.teach: Explain how the little ships helped at Dunkirk.

topics.title: Kings and queens
topics.intro: Britain has had kings and queens for more than a thousand years. Some were brave, some were clever, and one reigned for 70 years!
topics.talk: Ask {him} who is king now, and who was queen before.

items.prompt: Things that have already happened are in the…
items.explain: Past = already happened. Present = now. Future = still to come.

items.prompt: Things that have not happened yet are in the…
items.explain: Your next birthday is in the future.

items.prompt: Long ago, before electricity, how did people light their homes at night?

options.feedback: Light bulbs need electricity.
There were no phones long ago!

items.explain: Candles, oil lamps and later gas lamps lit homes before electricity.

items.prompt: Which toy would a child 100 years ago most likely have played with?

options.feedback: Games consoles are very recent.
These need batteries and electronics, invented much later.

items.explain: Old toys were often made of wood, tin or cloth: spinning tops, skipping ropes, marbles, dolls.

items.prompt: How did people wash clothes before washing machines?

options.feedback: They did, but it took a whole day!
Dishwashers are modern too.

items.explain: Washing day was hard work: scrubbing, rinsing and squeezing clothes through a mangle.

items.prompt: Put these in order, longest ago first.
items.explain: Romans (about 2,000 years ago), 1066, 1666, 1914, 1969.

items.prompt: How many years are in a century?
items.explain: A century is 100 years. A decade is 10.

items.prompt: About how long ago did the Romans invade Britain?
items.explain: The Romans invaded in AD 43, nearly 2,000 years ago.

items.prompt: Which city did the Romans come from?
items.explain: The Roman Empire was ruled from Rome, in Italy.

items.prompt: What was a Roman foot soldier called?
items.explain: Legionaries were tough, trained soldiers who marched about 30 km a day.

items.prompt: Roman soldiers made a “tortoise” (testudo) formation. What was it?

options.text: They made a shell of shields

options.feedback: It was named after the tortoise’s shell, not its speed!
That would be fun, but no!

items.explain: Locked shields made a shell that arrows and stones bounced off.

items.prompt: Which Roman emperor built a giant wall across the north of England?
items.explain: Hadrian’s Wall is about 117 km long. You can still walk along it today.

items.prompt: Which British warrior queen led a rebellion against the Romans?
items.explain: Boudica was queen of the Iceni tribe. Her army attacked Roman towns, including London, before the Romans defeated her.

items.prompt: Why were Roman roads so straight?

options.feedback: They could! Straight roads were just the fastest route.

options.text: To make the roads look prettier
options.feedback: Speed was the reason.

items.explain: Straight, well-built roads let the army move fast. Some modern roads follow them.

items.prompt: Which English city is named after its Roman baths?
items.explain: The Romans built baths around the hot springs there. You can still visit them.

items.prompt: What were the Vikings’ fast wooden ships called?
items.explain: Longships had sails and oars and could sail up rivers.

items.prompt: Where did the Vikings come from?
items.explain: Vikings came from Scandinavia, across the North Sea.

items.prompt: Which English king fought the Vikings and is called “the Great”?
items.explain: Alfred the Great was king of Wessex. A story says he once burned some cakes while hiding from the Vikings!

items.prompt: Did all Vikings just raid and fight?

options.text: No: many were farmers and traders

options.feedback: Many Vikings settled down and farmed. York was a big Viking town called Jorvik.
They did lots of things.

items.explain: Vikings were raiders, but also traders, farmers and explorers.

items.prompt: Did Vikings wear helmets with horns?
items.explain: Real Viking helmets were plain and rounded. The horns came from costumes in the 1800s.

items.prompt: In which year was the Battle of Hastings?
items.explain: 1066: one of the most famous dates in English history.

items.prompt: Who won the Battle of Hastings?
items.explain: William became known as William the Conqueror.

items.prompt: Which English king was killed at the Battle of Hastings?
items.explain: King Harold died in the battle. The Bayeux Tapestry shows a soldier with an arrow in his eye, which may be Harold.

items.prompt: What is the Bayeux Tapestry?
items.explain: It is about 70 metres long, like a giant comic strip made with wool.

items.prompt: William was crowned king on a special day in 1066. Which day?
items.explain: He was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

items.prompt: William’s army had soldiers on horseback. What were they called?
items.explain: Norman knights charged on horses. Harold’s army fought on foot behind a wall of shields.

items.prompt: What is the ditch of water around a castle called?
items.explain: A moat made it hard for attackers to reach the walls.

items.prompt: What is the bridge that could be lifted up to keep enemies out?
items.explain: Pulled up by chains, the drawbridge became an extra wall.

items.prompt: What is the heavy gate of wood and iron that slides down?
items.explain: The portcullis dropped down to block the entrance.

items.prompt: What is the strongest tower in the middle of a castle called?
items.explain: The keep was the safest place, where the lord lived.

items.prompt: The first Norman castles were “motte and bailey” castles. What were they made of?

options.text: wood, on a mound of earth

options.feedback: Glass would not keep anyone out!

options.text: blocks of ice, on a frozen lake
options.feedback: They would melt!

items.explain: They were quick to build from wood and earth. Later, stronger castles were made of stone.

items.prompt: Early knights wore armour made of tiny metal rings joined together. What was it called?
items.explain: Chainmail was flexible. Later knights wore solid plate armour.

items.prompt: A boy training to become a knight was called a…
items.explain: Boys started as pages, then became squires, then knights.

items.prompt: Knights painted a special design on their shield so people knew who they were. What was it called?
items.explain: In battle, helmets hid faces, so a coat of arms showed who was who.

items.prompt: In which year was the Great Fire of London?
items.explain: 1666, six hundred years after 1066.

items.prompt: Where did the Great Fire start?
items.answer: in a bakery on Pudding Lane
distractors: in a castle by the river
in a school on Bread Street
on a ship by London Bridge
items.explain: It started in Thomas Farriner’s bakery on Pudding Lane.

items.prompt: Why did the fire spread so quickly?

options.text: The wooden houses were close together
The fire brigade was on holiday
options.feedback: There was no proper fire brigade in 1666.

options.text: It was raining hard all week
options.feedback: Rain would have helped! It had been a dry summer.

items.explain: Wooden houses, a dry summer and a strong wind helped the fire spread.

items.prompt: For about how many days did the Great Fire burn?
items.explain: It burned from 2 to 6 September 1666.

items.prompt: Samuel Pepys wrote about the fire in his diary. What did he bury in his garden to keep it safe?
items.explain: He buried his cheese and his wine! His diary tells us a lot about the fire.

items.prompt: How did people finally stop the fire?

options.text: They pulled down houses to make gaps
They used fire engines with long hoses
options.feedback: There were no hoses like ours. They had leather buckets and hand squirts.

options.text: They waited for the snow to fall
options.feedback: It was September.

items.explain: Gaps called firebreaks stopped the flames, and the wind dropped.

items.prompt: Which famous cathedral burned down and was rebuilt by Christopher Wren?
items.explain: Wren’s new St Paul’s has a giant dome.

items.prompt: Who was Queen of England when the Spanish Armada came?
items.explain: Queen Elizabeth I reigned for 44 years.

items.prompt: In which year did the Armada sail?
What was the Armada?
items.answer: a huge fleet of Spanish warships
items.explain: About 130 ships sailed from Spain.

items.prompt: How did people warn the country that the Armada was coming?

options.text: They sent each other text messages
options.feedback: No phones in 1588!

options.text: They rang one bell in London
options.feedback: Beacons could be seen for miles.

items.explain: Each beacon was seen from the next hill, so the warning raced across England.

items.prompt: Which famous sailor helped to beat the Armada?
items.explain: A story says Drake finished his game of bowls before setting sail!

items.prompt: What were fireships?

options.text: Ships set on fire and sent at the enemy
Ships that put out fires at sea
options.feedback: They did the opposite!

options.text: Ships made out of magic fire
options.feedback: They were wooden ships set alight.

items.explain: The Spanish ships scattered to escape, and then storms wrecked many of them.

items.prompt: Who was known as “The Lady with the Lamp”?
items.explain: She checked on wounded soldiers at night, carrying a lamp.

items.prompt: In which war did Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole care for soldiers?
items.explain: The Crimean War was in the 1850s.

items.prompt: How did Florence Nightingale save lives?

options.text: She invented lots of new medicines
options.feedback: Her great idea was cleanliness.
She was a nurse, not a soldier.

items.explain: Dirty hospitals spread germs. Making them clean saved many lives.

items.prompt: Mary Seacole travelled from Jamaica and set up a place to care for soldiers near the battlefield. What did she call it?
items.explain: She gave soldiers food, comfort and medicine, sometimes right on the battlefield.

items.prompt: What did Florence Nightingale set up in London to train nurses?
items.explain: Her nursing school opened in 1860 at St Thomas’ Hospital.

items.prompt: When was the First World War?
items.explain: It lasted just over four years.

items.prompt: The fighting stopped at 11 o’clock on which day?
items.explain: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month. This is called the Armistice.

items.prompt: Why do we wear red poppies in November?

options.feedback: Poppies are a symbol of remembering.
That is 5 November. Poppies are for Remembrance.

items.explain: After the war, red poppies grew on the churned-up fields in Flanders, where many soldiers had fought.

items.prompt: On Remembrance Day, for how long do people stay silent?
items.explain: At 11 o’clock on 11 November, many people stop for two minutes’ silence.

items.prompt: Soldiers on the Western Front lived and fought in long ditches dug in the ground. What were they called?
items.explain: Trenches were muddy and cold. Soldiers took turns resting behind the front line.

items.prompt: What happened in some places at Christmas 1914?

options.text: Soldiers stopped fighting for a while

options.feedback: It went on until 1918.

options.text: Everyone went home for Christmas dinner
options.feedback: They stayed at the front, but some had a short truce.

items.explain: This is called the Christmas Truce: a moment of friendship between enemies.

items.prompt: Which new machine was first used in battle in 1916?
items.explain: Tanks could roll over trenches and barbed wire. The first ones were slow and very hot inside.

items.prompt: Which animals carried soldiers and pulled heavy guns in the First World War?
items.explain: Millions of horses worked in the war. Dogs and pigeons carried messages too.

items.prompt: When was the Second World War?
items.explain: It lasted six years.

items.prompt: Who was the British Prime Minister for most of the Second World War?
items.explain: Churchill gave famous speeches to keep people brave.

items.prompt: What was an evacuee?

options.text: A child sent to the countryside
A soldier who flew a plane
options.feedback: Evacuees were mostly children.
Evacuees were people.

items.explain: Children travelled by train with a label, a gas mask and a small suitcase, to live with families in safer places.

items.prompt: What was the Blitz?
items.explain: The Blitz was in 1940 and 1941. People sheltered when the air-raid siren sounded.

items.prompt: What were the small metal shelters people built in their gardens called?
items.explain: They were half buried in the ground and covered with earth to protect families.

items.prompt: Why did families have ration books?

options.text: So everyone got a fair share of food

options.feedback: They were for sharing food fairly.

options.text: To borrow books from the library
options.feedback: Ration books were for food.

items.explain: Ships bringing food were attacked, so food like sugar, butter and meat was rationed.

items.prompt: People were asked to grow their own vegetables. What was the slogan?
items.explain: Parks and gardens were turned into vegetable patches.

items.prompt: Which famous British fighter plane flew in the Battle of Britain?
items.explain: Spitfires and Hurricanes of the RAF defended Britain’s skies in 1940.

items.prompt: Why did people cover their windows at night during the “blackout”?
items.answer: so enemy planes could not see
items.explain: With no lights showing, it was harder for bombers to find their targets.

items.prompt: VE Day was when the war in Europe ended. How did people celebrate?
items.explain: VE Day was 8 May 1945. People danced, sang and shared food in the streets.

items.prompt: Which two brothers made the first powered aeroplane flight in 1903?
items.explain: Orville Wright flew for 12 seconds. The plane was called the Flyer.

items.prompt: Which brave British pilot was the first woman to fly alone from England to Australia, in 1930?
items.explain: She flew in a small plane called Jason. The trip took 19 days.

items.prompt: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
items.explain: Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, and he stepped out a few hours later (early on 21 July, UK time). Buzz Aldrin stepped out next.

items.prompt: What was the name of a famous early steam train, built by George and Robert Stephenson in 1829?
items.explain: Stephenson’s Rocket won a race to find the best locomotive, at nearly 30 miles per hour!

items.prompt: Put these firsts in order, earliest first.
In 1940, hundreds of “little ships” (fishing boats and pleasure boats) sailed across the Channel to rescue soldiers. Where from?
items.explain: More than 300,000 soldiers were brought home from the beaches of Dunkirk in France.

items.prompt: Where did codebreakers work in secret to crack enemy messages?
items.explain: Clever people there, including Alan Turing, built machines to help crack codes.

items.prompt: Which brilliant mathematician helped crack enemy codes and is now called a father of the computer?
items.explain: Turing is on the £50 note.

items.prompt: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, soldiers landed on the beaches of which country?
items.explain: Soldiers from Britain, America, Canada and other countries landed in Normandy to begin freeing Europe.

items.prompt: Which animals carried secret messages and some even won medals for bravery?
items.explain: Pigeons and dogs received the Dickin Medal, a medal for brave animals.

items.prompt: Which princess, who later became queen, trained as a mechanic and army lorry driver in the war?
items.explain: She joined the Auxiliary Territorial Service in 1945 and learned to fix engines.

items.prompt: What is a king or queen called?
items.explain: Monarch means one ruler.

items.prompt: Which queen reigned for 70 years, longer than any other British monarch?
items.explain: Queen Elizabeth II reigned from 1952 to 2022.

items.prompt: Who became king in 2022?
items.explain: King Charles III is Queen Elizabeth II’s eldest son.

items.prompt: Which queen reigned for 63 years in the 1800s and gave her name to a whole period of history?
items.explain: The Victorian age had steam trains, factories and big changes.

items.prompt: Which Tudor king had six wives?
items.explain: “Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived.”

items.prompt: Where are the Crown Jewels kept?
items.explain: The Tower of London is a castle built by William the Conqueror.
